articles.title: Guilfoyle scandal adds to scrutiny surrounding Trump advisers
articles.summary: President Trump faces a scandal involving a top official, with Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle under scrutiny for allegedly soliciting debt relief in exchange for political access. That revelation follows other reported questionable conduct, including favoring a Greek energy firm. It was the second time this week a White House adviser drew headlines. The Trump…
articles.body:
President Trump faces a scandal involving a top official, with Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle under scrutiny for allegedly soliciting debt relief in exchange for political access. That revelation follows other reported questionable conduct, including favoring a Greek energy firm.

It was the second time this week a White House adviser drew headlines.

The Trump administration appeared caught off guard by the reports involving Guilfoyle.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, on a diplomatic trip to Greece, bristled at reporters’ questions over whether he maintained confidence in Guilfoyle and whether her conduct raised any concerns.

“Like, our job is not to respond every time someone decides to give the media something without any advance warning, without having any chance to look at it and see what’s in there,” he said.

While the administration is batting away questions about Guilfoyle, Democrats have put the ambassador in the crosshairs.

“Reports coming out regarding Amb. Guilfoyle’s conduct are deeply concerning and suggest potentially corrupt influences on U.S. foreign policy,” Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) said in a statement to The Hill. “I have already demanded answers from Secretary [Marco] Rubio regarding her conduct and will continue to press for transparency and accountability. As I have said before, if these allegations are accurate, Amb. Guilfoyle is unfit to represent the United States abroad and should be removed from her position.”

The Wall Street Journal first reported Wednesday that Guilfoyle asked one of Trump’s donors to wire her $100,000 to cover her credit card debt in a way that would not show up in paperwork ahead of her confirmation hearing for ambassador to Greece.

In text messages obtained by NewsNation, the partner site for The Hill, Guilfoyle pleads for the donor, Eric Deters, to wire the funds to American Express.

“It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express,” she wrote on Signal on July 3, 2025, according to messages reviewed by The Hill. Her confirmation hearing took place July 9, 2025.

Deters said Guilfoyle offered to be his “ride or die in Trump world” if he made the credit card payment, according to a dossier he compiled and shared with NewsNation.

NewsNation reached out to Guilfoyle’s lawyer for comment.

Jesse Binnall, a lawyer for Guilfoyle, told the Journal that the ambassador disputed the authenticity of the messages but declined to provide specifics. Binnall said Guilfoyle was owed a balance related to speaking events, which Deters disputed.

The chaos around Guilfoyle was a “clown show,” which “tainted” a successful visit by Rubio to Greece, said one person deeply involved in U.S. and Greek relations speaking with The Hill on condition of anonymity.

The person said Guilfoyle’s conduct is unlikely to impact what are long-standing and deep ties between Washington and Athens, but that it reinforced the idea of that U.S. foreign policy is for sale and that ties to Trump’s family and close allies equals access.

“It says, ‘we’re the merchants,’” the person said.

Lawmakers and former ambassadors have called on her to be investigated and fired.

“Ambassador Guilfoyle must be fired and if she broke the law, which seems highly likely, prosecuted,” Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), who served as ambassador to Switzerland and Lichtenstein in the Obama administration, posted on social platform X.

Beyer pointed out that “accepting large sums of cash in exchange for access or favors using her official position would obviously run afoul” of federal laws and regulations.

The Daily Mail reported Thursday that sources said the State Department Office of Inspector General is investigating complaints into Guilfoyle and conduct at the U.S. Embassy in Athens.

The State Department office told The Hill it doesn’t comment on investigations.

Donald K. Sherman, president of ethics watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), said Rubio must demand an investigation.

“Guilfoyle’s alleged conduct is emblematic of the dangers posed when government officials cozying up to wealthy political interests as President Trump and his appointees have done time and time again. Influence seekers gaining financial leverage over American officials and diplomats is an unacceptable national security risk that threatens our interests abroad and safety at home,” Sherman said in a statement.

The controversy and scrutiny surrounding Guilfoyle add to a growing list of allegations of graft and conflicts of interest for Trump family members and administration advisers.

This includes questions swirling about two Trump advisers, James Blair and Chris LaCivita, who The New York Times reported this week were paid to advise a pro-Russia political party in Republika Srpska, a small self-governing territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Trump issued a rare public rebuke against the two men , close aides to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. Trump called them “outside consultants” and added that if there’s conflict of interest, he “will terminate them, immediately!”

But he has not publicly remarked on reports about Guilfoyle. The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

Another top Trump official under scrutiny for mixing government work and personal business is Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law. He serves as a top envoy for peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine and with Iran.

Kushner was the subject of a September profile in The New Yorker that laid out the myriad and overlapping potential conflicts of interest between his diplomacy portfolio and investments from Middle East monarchies and influential regional billionaires.

Kushner pushed back in a lengthy “fact check” post, disputing that his diplomatic work has benefited his business dealings, in particular his private investment firm Affinity Partners, which has received significant investment from Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and an Emirati-based investment firm , among others.

“Over the past decade, no one has identified a single American position I changed, government favor I sought, or diplomatic decision I made in order to benefit myself, Affinity, or one of its investors,” he wrote .

“Allegations of conflicts should ultimately be tested against specifics: What action did I take, whose financial interest did it benefit, and what evidence shows that the two were connected? Generalized suspicion is not a substitute for answering those questions.”

And last month, Trump defended his son Donald Trump Jr., who permitted a Russian oligarch, Umar Kremlev, to pay hundreds of thousands of dollars related to his wedding, including for help renting a private island and putting on a fireworks display. The president said his son would pay back the oligarch. Kremlev told a press conference Tuesday that Trump Jr. did pay him back but maintained his lavish spending was a wedding gift.

The wedding gift controversy came amid a scrutiny of Trump Jr.’s other international business dealings, including promotion of family-backed cryptocurrency ventures, international real estate deals involving direct meetings with foreign heads of state and reported investments in defense contracting. Trump Jr. also has significant ties to prediction market platforms that depend on favorable regulatory decisions by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, The New York Times reported in January.

These allegations featured prominently in a letter sent by Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) to Senate Judiciary Committee Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), requesting an investigation into Trump Jr. as seriously as Republicans looked into Hunter Biden, President Biden’s son who was criticized for business ventures in Ukraine while his father was vice president.

“The country should not have to accept one standard for the family of a Republican president and another for the family of a Democratic president. Nor should congressional oversight begin and end when control of the White House changes hands,” Curtis wrote in the letter.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said Thursday that Guilfoyle, LaCivita and Blair “need to answer a lot of questions” following the recent reports.

“On its face, it’s at best horrible optics, and at worst, something that’s worthy of a termination,” Tillis told CNN’s Wolf Blitzer on “The Situation Room.”

He said he was willing to give them the “benefit of the doubt but those are very clearly legitimate questions that should be asked [by] members of Congress.”

While Curtis and Tillis — who is retiring in January — are rare GOP critics, Democrats are readying investigations into Trump and his advisers’ business dealings if they win the majority after the midterm elections. Majority control comes with subpoena power.

“Trump’s ambassador to Greece is the latest Mar-a-Lago Mafia member caught selling access. She won’t be the last. We must expose all the Trump cartel’s corruption,” Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Va.), a member of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, posted on X .

articles.title: Autism providers warn foster kids at risk from unintended consequences of Trump's Medicaid fraud crackdown
articles.summary: Georgia foster families face losing autism therapy access as providers warn the government's Medicaid cuts go too far in the name of fraud prevention.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: American autism care providers who backed the Trump administration's crackdown on Medicaid fraud are now sounding the alarm, warning that efforts to root out abuse could have unintended consequences after reimbursement cuts put therapy for Georgia foster children at risk. The Autism Families Alliance, which describes itself as a national advocacy organization dedicated to supporting Applied Behavior Analysis providers and the families who rely on their services, said that efforts by the Trump administration and state leaders to fight fraud have gone too far, potentially leaving many of Georgia's children with autism in foster care without the care they need. This warning is in response to a move by Amerigroup, the insurer that covers Georgia’s foster children through Medicaid, to cut what it pays autism therapy providers by 30%. Providers caution that they may no longer be able to afford to treat vulnerable children and that many foster families will be unable to switch them to another insurer. "It's scary to see that so many different things are being slashed in terms of Medicaid, and that we're seeing this drastic outcome," Taylor Sanders, a family advocate at the Autism Families Alliance, told Fox News Digital. "It's so important that we keep in mind that children with autism are in a very vulnerable place where they're still needing to learn safety skills. There are some children who have extremely aggressive behaviors, challenging behaviors. So, when we're seeing some of these cuts, we're seeing it affect the providers who are able to provide access to these services." AUTISM PROVIDERS CHEER TRUMP CRACKDOWN AFTER MILLIONS ALLEGEDLY STOLEN THROUGH MEDICAID FRAUD "If we're not able to provide a good amount of pay to our providers, we're not able to make sure they're set up for success to be able to give some of these services, and we're going to see less and less children being able to access services at all," she added. Sanders said 75% of clinics will have to close their doors or stop serving foster kids due to the massive cuts. The 30% cut will not only affect providers' ability to provide access to these families, but it will also limit foster children's opportunities to learn essential skills, according to Sanders. Foster children with autism depend on regular therapy to develop everyday skills, but a sudden loss of that support could set them back. "If they don't learn these school skills at an early intervention or an early age, it'll be a lot more costly later on," she said. In August, the Autism Families Alliance put its support behind the Trump administration's crackdown on Medicaid fraud, arguing that the alleged theft of millions of federal funds has hurt both taxpayers and children with autism who rely on those services. Some states, including Georgia, have also taken steps to enhance oversight of autism services. The group backed eliminating fraud and prosecuting suspected criminals, but also feared that broad federal and state efforts to root out fraud could unintentionally make it more difficult for legitimate providers to care for children with autism. The coalition called on policymakers to ensure fraudsters are removed from the system without creating what they described as unnecessary barriers for families of vulnerable children seeking care. RFK JR ANNOUNCES 'LARGEST AUTISM FRAUD BUST IN AMERICAN HISTORY' WITH $46.6M MEDICAID SCHEME INDICTMENT Now, the group says Georgia’s foster families face the risk that they had previously raised concerns about. "I think fraud should be prosecuted by all means," Sanders said. "Anybody who is engaging in fraudulent behavior should be prosecuted to the highest extent of the law. Are we able to not only tackle the fraud, but still give access to services for our children? Why can't we do both at the same time?" "What's really happening here is we're going in with a sledgehammer when really we should be going in with a scalpel," she continued, adding that officials need to be "approaching this in a way where it's not going to totally obliterate the care to our families." One Georgia foster mother has already been told her nearly 3-year-old son’s provider may be forced to stop treating him after he started making progress, according to the Georgia Recorder. "Reforms that improve care, increase efficiency and prevent abuse are something we all support, but when those efforts make it harder for children with autism to get the care they need, something has gone terribly wrong," Kelsey Bennett, a family advocate with the Autism Families Alliance, told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "No one wants to eliminate waste, fraud and abuse more than the providers who dedicate their lives to caring for these children. Every taxpayer dollar should go toward helping the people it was intended to serve. But you can't fix a system by making it harder for vulnerable children to get help. Reforms that end up hurting the very children the system is supposed to protect are not in Georgia's best interests," she continued. Bennett urged Georgia's lawmakers "to bring everyone to the table, including the Medicaid managed care companies and the providers who care for these children every day." "By listening to those on the front lines and working together, they can find a better way forward that improves efficiency without putting children's access to care at risk," she said. "Children with autism, especially those in foster care and those welcomed into loving foster families, already face enough challenges. Their families shouldn't have to worry about whether the care they depend on will suddenly disappear. Georgia's leaders need to step in, address these cuts and make sure these children aren't the ones paying the price for efforts to save money," she added.

articles.title: The powerful way American communities can benefit from the new tech boom revealed by data center CEO
articles.summary: Compass Datacenters CEO Chris Crosby details how the Red Oak, Texas, campus created 900 jobs, an animal shelter and a skilled trades training facility.
articles.body: RED OAK, Texas — A data center firm is taking a very different approach by integrating into the communities where they build the massive facilities needed to power Americans' technology and support the growing artificial intelligence (AI) boom. As these centers face flak over growing concerns about their impact on resources and infrastructure, Compass Datacenters CEO Chris Crosby tells Fox News Digital that it's up to companies like his to work with communities, identify local needs, plan improvements and invest in projects that benefit residents. And that's what he aimed to do from the start when building out a hyperscale data center campus in a town of approximately 20,000 people just 20 miles south of Dallas. Crosby detailed how he was able to create a data center with "no noise, no light pollution" and a completely water-free cooling system. "Do you need a fire truck? Do you need a new school? Do you need baseball fields for your community?" Crosby proposed in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital. "These are important capital investments that can really boost a community, and many communities should be asking for those things." ONE SOUTHERN STATE’S RISE IS MAKING IT AMERICA’S NEW ‘ECONOMIC CENTER OF GRAVITY’ "When you think about durability and putting a hundred-year-type asset into a community, you better do that really well and in conjunction with that community," he added. In Red Oak, Compass donated $15 million to build an animal shelter after the SPCA ended its contract in the town last year, Crosby said. His company also partnered with Texas State Technical College on a $12.6 million training facility to expand the school’s Mechanical, Electrical and IT Data Center Pathway program. The 12-week course is designed to help people enter skilled trades and technical careers that data centers rely on. The work includes electricians, mechanics and technicians, as well as construction trades such as carpentry, welding and concrete work. Crosby said the program is open to people without prior qualifications and prepares them for careers across the industry. "We can’t get enough people into this career," he said. "Unfortunately, there was a war on blue-collar jobs a while back and everybody had to get a four-year degree. I’m so glad that’s over with." Compass began developing its Red Oak campus in 2019. It now includes 10 data center buildings, a Schneider Electric manufacturing facility and the training center. Crosby said about 900 people work on site — roughly 600 for Compass and 300 for Schneider Electric — in addition to the thousands of construction workers who have worked on the project over the past five years. AMERICA’S NEW BLUE-COLLAR JOB BOOM IS ONE NOBODY SAW COMING — AND IT’S JUST GETTING STARTED "I am tired of the elitism that this doesn’t create jobs," Crosby said of his sprawling data center and the rhetoric that they do not bring lasting American jobs. "You tell that to the 900 people who work here on this campus, and you tell that to the thousands of construction workers who have worked here for five years plus," he added. The jobs and community investments are one side of a debate playing out across the country. As data centers expand nationwide, their electricity and water use — and the strain they can place on local infrastructure — are drawing growing scrutiny. But Crosby said Compass has not used water to cool its data centers since the company began operating, a choice he said is personal and practical. "We haven’t used water since inception, because I grew up in North Texas. I know water is a precious resource," he said. At the Red Oak facility, water is used only for bathrooms, according to Compass. The company uses a hybrid cooling system that can operate with air or liquid cooling. Crosby said avoiding water cooling can reduce efficiency, but he considers the trade-off worthwhile. Crosby said Compass favors connecting to the grid and believes data center companies can help pay for transmission and generation upgrades. "We think that we can contribute to the infrastructure for the grid," he said, adding that data center companies can "co-invest" in upgrades. He also said facilities could help reduce peak demand and grid congestion by adjusting when they draw power. At Red Oak, Crosby said Compass donated seven parcels to the transmission provider to route power lines without using eminent domain. He said that also means controlling noise and light pollution and meeting EPA noise limits at the property line. "It’s very important to be a quiet neighbor — no noise, no light pollution, and, of course, taking care of the precious resources that are there in that community," he said.

articles.body: First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli called out California Democrats for watering down the state's criminal law after federal law enforcement led the charge on a massive drug crackdown in the infamous Skid Row neighborhood on Thursday. Essayli told Fox News Digital in an interview that California's state and local law enforcement have worked with the feds just fine, but that it's the politicians who are getting in the way. "Unfortunately, states like California have totally watered down their laws, their criminal justice laws. They've also emptied their prisons and closed prisons, so effectively, there's not much of a deterrence on the state side. No one faces any serious consequences on the state side," Essayli said. NEWSOM BLASTED BY SHERIFF IN HIS OWN BACKYARD OVER CALIFORNIA CRIME AS VICTIMS CRY FOUL "We work really well with our local law enforcement partners," he continued. It's more the governor, it's the legislature, it's these loud-mouth federal, you know, Congress members who all they care about is attacking the administration, attacking the president." Essayli did give credit to Mayor Karen Bass for approving the Los Angeles Police Department to participate in Thursday's Operation Save Skid Row. articles.title: El-Sayed vs. Rogers gets nasty in Michigan
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Nobel Peace Prize awarded ▪ Trump says no Iran strikes before midterms ▪ Kimberly Guilfoyle’s debt controversy ▪ Spain’s housing movement reignited The Michigan Senate debate between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers on Thursday night quickly got personal as the candidates sparred over not just their political differences but…
articles.body:
▪ Trump says no Iran strikes before midterms

The Michigan Senate debate between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers on Thursday night quickly got personal as the candidates sparred over not just their political differences but their personal backgrounds.

The debate, hosted by Nexstar affiliate WOOD-TV in Grand Rapids and NewsNation, is the first of two debates they will take part in before Election Day; the next one will take place on Oct. 21. Nexstar also owns The Hill.

El-Sayed, a former Wayne County health director, and Rogers, a former congressman, repeatedly interrupted each other during the hourlong debate. The event was so contentious that the candidates’ arguments continued even during the brief commercial break.

“I n 30 years of doing debates, I’ve never seen it continue during the commercial, but it did,” said moderator Rick Albin .

El-Sayed’s attacks on Rogers largely focused on accusations that he would be a “rubber stamp” for President Trump and corporate interests and was carpetbagging with his Senate bid.

“I’ve been absolutely clear. I want our tax dollars spent here to provide schools here, and by here, I mean Michigan, not Florida,” El-Sayed said.

Rogers had lived in Michigan for years and represented the state during his time in the House but had moved to Florida before his first unsuccessful Senate run in 2024.

The Republican nominee’s attacks on El-Sayed ranged from accusations that he was misrepresenting himself as a medical professional to baselessly alleging that he could have terrorist family members.

El-Sayed has received a medical degree from Columbia University and a doctorate in public health from Oxford University but had received scrutiny for calling himself a “physician” despite not practicing medicine.

When Rogers was asked about his position on guardrails surrounding Flock cameras, he said they were important in catching people suspected of terrorism.

“And why would that bother you? Well, if you have someone in your family that might be on —” he said, before El-Sayed cut in.

“Go ahead and say it,” El-Sayed said. “You’ve been tiptoeing around it the whole time, just say it.”

Other major Senate debates taking place simultaneously also got into testy territory with personal swipes.

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Maine Democratic nominee Troy Jackson demanded apologies from each other after Jackson claimed that she and her husband have profited from the Iran war. Jackson didn’t offer specific evidence for his claim. Reporting from The Maine Independent has revealed that Collins’s husband owns stock in defense contractors.

“I mean, Senator Collins and her husband [are] making money, more, off of this war, and so is a whole bunch of other people, and that’s why this doesn’t, doesn’t stop,” Jackson said.

“That is absolutely outrageous, and you owe me an apology,” the senator shot back.

“No, you owe me an apology,” Jackson responded.

Personal accusations also flew in the Georgia Senate debate , with Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) denouncing GOP nominee Rep. Mike Collins (Ga.) as a “bigot.”

“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club,” Ossoff said, referencing past social media posts from Collins.

One such post included a video from the University of Mississippi in 2024 in which a Black woman is surrounded by white students who mimic ape-like motions and make monkey sounds.

“Ole Miss taking care of business,” Collins wrote at the time.

Ossoff also accused Collins of promoting “neo-Nazi” propaganda. Collins responded that he condemns racism, antisemitism and hate.

The congressman hit back at Ossoff, calling him a “trust fund kid” who doesn’t understand the financial struggles that average people are dealing with.

“You know the problem is, and Jon Ossoff won’t understand this because he doesn’t have to worry about health care,” Collins said. “He doesn’t have to worry about trying to buy health care insurance for his family. He never will.”

Ossoff responded that Collins “inherited” his seat in Congress, as the congressman’s father was Mac Collins , who served in the House for 12 years.

A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot and wounded a man Thursday in New York City. Officials told NewsNation that the man is an immigrant who entered the country illegally and has a criminal record. The man was transported to a local hospital .

The USS Abraham Lincoln docked in San Diego Thursday after a grueling 322-day deployment to the Middle East , marked by dwindling food supplies and concerns over service members’ mental health. The deployment, expected to end in the summer, was extended to support the Iran war.

The Trump administration unveiled new charges against deposed Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, accusing them of ordering the torture of Americans and political opponents. The duo previously pleaded not guilty to charges related to narco-terrorism and cocaine trafficking.

U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Navi Pillay speaks at a media briefing in Colombo, Sri Lanka, Saturday, Aug. 31, 2013. (AP Photo/Eranga Jayawardena)

NOBEL WIN : The Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the Nobel Peace Prize to former United Nations human rights chief Navanethem “Navi” Pillay on Friday, recognizing her efforts to promote peace and international law.

Pillay, 85, is a judge on the International Court of Justice. She led the U.N. human rights commission for six years, from 2008 to 2014, and previously served as the president of the international tribunal on the Rwandan genocide for four years.

In remarks to colleagues after receiving the award, she noted that her most recent work was a report naming Israel’s war in Gaza as a genocide.

Jørgen Watne Frydnes , the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, said Pillay’s work is a “source of hope and inspiration to all those who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.”

This year marks the 125th anniversary of the prize.

It comes a year after Trump and some of his allies launched a concerted campaign for him to be awarded the prize, pointing to his efforts for peace in various international conflicts. This year, the president’s camp was relatively quiet, though he was asked about whether he deserved the prize earlier this week.

“I settled eight wars. Another one is coming. I got all the hostages back,” he said. “I did things that nobody else has ever done. I’m not bragging. I’m just telling you the facts.”

Last year’s winner, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado , gave her prize to Trump soon after the U.S. operation that ousted former dictator Nicolás Maduro in January. But the committee has said the award can’t be transferred.

Pillay nodded to the exchange in her comments on Friday.

“If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” she said to laughs.

OFF THE TABLE: Trump said Thursday the U.S. military would not launch any attacks on Iran before the midterm elections after reporting that the president was weighing whether to resume major combat operations before Election Day.

“I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect, with Oil flowing in Record Numbers of Barrels through the Hormuz Strait (22 Million Barrels, last night alone, with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran!), we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Oil prices rose earlier Thursday following reporting from The Atlantic that the White House asked the Pentagon to develop strike options against Iranian targets that could be exercised before the midterms. U.S. officials also told Axios that U.S. Central Command was instructed to finalize its preparations to resume combat operations in Iran, but that no final decisions had been made.

Asked about the reporting earlier Thursday, a White House official told The Hill that Trump “has all options available at any time.”

“Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways; the easy way or the hard way. President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States,” the official said.

VISA CRACKDOWN : Vice President Vance announced new efforts to crack down on alleged fraud and abuse in work visa programs, including a probe into nine universities over their use of the J-1 visa program and the suspension of Microsoft and other tech companies from an employer-based program that allows foreign workers to apply for permanent resident status.

“Elite universities bring in foreigners to undercut the wages of American residents,” Vance said at a press conference yesterday, noting American graduate students make roughly $20,000 more than their foreign counterparts. He accused the nine universities of using J-1 visa holders for federally funded research at a rate of 61 percent, compared with a national average of 38 percent.

Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito said “subpoenas have been served” to the nine schools, which include Harvard University, Yale University, Stanford University, Brown University, the University of Pittsburgh, Arizona State University, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the California Institute of Technology and the University of California, Davis.

The vice president separately announced that Microsoft has been suspended from the permanent labor certification program, accusing the tech giant of relying heavily on foreign workers while laying off thousands of Americans. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys and several other IT firms were also suspended from the program.

Microsoft pushed back, saying the “vast majority” of its U.S. employees are Americans.

STAND BY : A federal judge temporarily extended a pause Thursday on the White House’s ban of three media outlets from covering the president as he considers a longer block against the move.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly , a Trump appointee, said his initial 14-day order, which was set to expire just before midnight, will be extended another two business days. A ruling is expected by Tuesday.

Kelly didn’t address the arguments from CNN, MS NOW and Politico that the ban violates their First Amendment rights, as Trump said he barred them from the White House grounds because of cumulative negative coverage. Instead, he found the ban likely violates their constitutional due process rights.

CNN and Politico have since been blocked from traveling on Air Force One as part of press pool duties, adding another front in the standoff.

▪ The Hill : John Roberts halts deadline for FCC to rule on TV ad rate challenge.

NO COMMENT : Secretary of State Marco Rubio deflected on questions about The Wall Street Journal report that U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle solicited cash from a GOP donor to pay off debts during her confirmation process.

“Our job is not to respond every time someone decides to give the media something without any advance warning, without having any chance to look at it and see what’s in there,” he said.

The outlet reported on messages sent on Signal in which Guilfoyle asked Eric Deters to send her $100,000 to pay off debts to American Express in a way that wouldn’t leave a paper trail.

Guilfoyle reportedly asked Deters to wire her the money in July 2025, six days before her confirmation hearing in front of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. Deters ultimately turned her down.

“Your needing $100,000 urgent unfortunately is not going to work,” Deters reportedly wrote to Guilfoyle. “I can’t do this without getting a divorce.”

The House will convene at 12:30 p.m. for a pro forma session.

The Senate will meet at 1:30 p.m. for a pro forma session.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., arrives on stage at the inaugural Make America Healthy Again summit, Nov. 12, 2025, in Washington. (Rod Lamkey, Jr., Associated Press file)

MAHA BACKLASH : Frustration is growing among Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) activists over what some see as serious betrayals by Republican officials they helped put in office, raising concerns for the GOP just weeks away from the midterms, The Hill’s Rachel Frazin and Nathaniel Weixel report .

The latest rift between MAHA supporters and certain GOP allies is over the farm bill, which is supported by Republicans who purport to support the movement. But activists are taking issue with cuts in the bill to certain conservation programs and with a provision to delay a deadline for the Environmental Protection Agency to re-review the health impacts of pesticides that are already on the market.

MAHA supporters have rallied around opposition to vaccine mandates and concerns about the influence of chemical and agricultural companies on public health policy, leaving some activists torn over whom to support in the midterms.

“Do we vote for someone who supports vaccine mandates … or do we vote for someone who is actively supporting pesticides and poison in our foods that our babies and children eat on a daily basis?” Zen Honeycutt , founder of Moms Across America, told Frazin and Weixel. “It’s an impossible decision, and this is why many of our moms are saying they’re going to stay home, or vote independent, write somebody in.”

Another tension point came at the MAHA Summit last week, when Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — the face of the MAHA movement — and other administration officials mingled with executives from drug developers, insurers, AI companies and retailers like Walmart.

“The people who built this movement were promised an end to … Washington influence-peddling, not a MAHA-branded version of it,” Robert Malone , a former vice chair of Kennedy’s vaccine advisory committee, wrote in a scathing blog post titled “The Capture of MAHA.”

Flowers, candles and farewell messages are placed at a memorial in Madrid, Spain, to honor the memory of Maria del Carmen Abascal, 87, whose eviction from her home sparked nationwide protests, Oct. 8, 2026. (Manu Fernandez, Associated Press)

SYMBOL OF THE MOVEMENT : The death of an 87-year-old Spanish woman whose eviction sparked national protests in Spain is renewing the social movement demanding action on the country’s housing crisis.

María del Carmen Abascal , who became widely known as “Maricarmen,” died Wednesday in a hospital , two weeks after she was evicted from her home where she had lived for decades before her rent spiked. Her lawyer didn’t reveal her cause of death.

Spaniards have been increasingly frustrated by rising housing costs for months, but the televised images of Maricarmen being carried on a stretcher from her home provoked fierce backlash. She had used a wheelchair.

The incident spurred thousands of demonstrators to protest in Madrid and other major cities in Spain. Protesters in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol square held a minute of silence in Maricarmen’s honor upon learning of her death.

Her situation helped ignite a social movement that has effectively spurred an early general election scheduled for Nov. 29, eight months earlier than originally expected, as Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez hopes to seize the momentum to win a new mandate.

Sánchez took a defeat last week as right-wing opposition parties were able to defeat emergency measures introduced by his government to address evictions and the difficult real estate market.

His gambit risks providing a path to victory for a right-wing coalition made up of conservatives and the far-right Vox party.

“All my love to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones,” Sánchez said in a post on the social platform X. “A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today. Rest in peace.”

Labor unions have meanwhile called for a general strike in the two weeks leading up to the election.

“Your death won’t be in vain. We will continue the struggle,” one of the messages on Maricarmen’s door reads.

articles.title: Whole Hog Politics: What kind of polling miss can Republicans expect?

Members can join the discussion and pose their questions to Bill and Chris. Tune in!] The House is looking enough like a done deal…
articles.body:
[ Watch Whole Hog Politics Live : Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. ET as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon go deep on this week’s political news. Members can join the discussion and pose their questions to Bill and Chris. Tune in! ]

The House is looking enough like a done deal for Democrats that even the relentlessly positive Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is musing publicly about what comes next for him if Republicans get the boot in November.

So, how’s it going for Republicans’ bid to keep the Senate?

Oil prices rose Thursday on reports that the Pentagon was preparing for an imminent, large-scale attack on Iran. President Trump responded on social media saying, “We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd.”

This is an odd thing to say, even by the president’s standards. He knows that the high price of energy and its knock-on effects in other products are part of what is killing his party’s already dim midterm chances. Perhaps the calculation is that if he pledges not to attack, he could prevent the spike in futures prices that would be hitting consumers in the next few weeks. But for a president of the United States to explicitly, publicly tie military decisions to an election is a new one, as far as I know.

Whatever it was, it didn’t seem to work. After a brief pause in the rally, prices started climbing again. Do traders not believe the president? Do they assume that he might reverse himself in another post available early to paid subscribers ? Do they just figure that not bombing now means that inevitable November strikes will be all the bigger and that 25 days isn’t very long to hedge against that possibility?

Maybe the message was aimed more directly at voters, with whom the Iran war has been hugely unpopular. But there, it’s a puzzler, too. Saying you won’t do an unpopular thing before an election implies that you are inclined to do it after . And, again, unless it is a trick to mask a sudden strike, it surely can’t have been aimed at the Iranians who must not be able to believe their good luck in facing off with an American president so constantly whipsawed by polls and markets.

It’s a small episode in a larger story about how the already terrible campaign climate for Republicans keeps finding new depths of despair. Every day, in ways large and small, the environment in which the remaining persuadable voters are making up their minds is flashing big, red down arrows for the party in power.

We start every election cycle with, say, 80 percent of votes accounted for. The remaining 20 percent of the electorate is sorted out from those who decide to just stay home. Many of that fifth of voters make their minds up early on, often as soon as primary elections are concluded. The final fight is over that last 5 percent or so who just can’t quite make up their minds. Lots of things may affect those choices, but none so much as the overall climate in which the decisions are being made.

So what is the actual climate for Republicans scrambling to save the Senate? There we turn to the generic ballot: polls measuring voters’ expressed preference for partisan control of Congress. The correlation with the House vote is much tighter because as good and bad nominees in Senate races this year continue to prove, candidate quality matters a great deal more for the upper chamber.

In the most recent average of high-quality polls, Democrats enjoy an advantage of 9.6 points over Republicans. That would mean that the swing states are all going blue and the 10 or so least-red red states have turned purple. Certainly, there’s evidence for that as we see Republicans pouring money into states that haven’t elected a Democratic senator this century.

But, Republicans will say, the polls are wrong and that Republicans will again be understated, as they were in 2024 and 2020, and the “shy Trump voters” will turn out and close the gap. If the polls were as far off this cycle as they were in 2024, Republicans would still be trailing Democrats by 7.1 points in this year’s generic ballot instead of 9.6 points. That might matter if you’re a Senate Republican running in those 10 red states, but still a pretty garbage-y environment for the GOP overall.

But we know we shouldn’t compare midterms to presidential years. The turnout levels are just too different for useful comparisons.

Let’s say polling error this year was identical in size and direction as it was in the previous midterm cycle. The final average in 2022 showed Democrats getting 46.6 percent of the House vote and Republicans getting 49 percent. Both were understated, Democrats by 1.2 points and Republicans by 1.6 points. Apply that to the current average, and the Democrats would be ahead now by 9.2 points. Not a significant improvement.

But, Democrats would say, you can’t compare a good(ish) Republican midterm year with a bad Republican year. OK, how about 2018? That year, the polls understated Republicans by even more: 2.3 points compared with 1.5 points for Democrats. Things stay about the same, but with a slightly better outcome for the GOP: Democrats lead by 8.8 points.

That’s not exactly right, either. In 2018, it was Trump’s first midterm, and he still had a lot more of his mojo. Second-term midterms have been a very different animal in recent decades. It’s much harder to keep a coalition together as a lame duck. So how about 2006, a bad Republican year in a Republican president’s second term.

And, sure enough, 2006 had the largest midterm polling miss on Republicans of any of the relevant cycles: almost a full 3 points, while Democrats almost perfectly matched their pre-election final average, outperforming by just .8 points.

If you apply those misses to the current averages, you get the smallest Democratic advantage at 7.5 points.

You’re probably seeing the trend here. History tells us that Republicans are likely to be more understated in polls than Democrats, but the previous misses are nowhere near enough to say anything other than that this is looking like a very tough cycle for the GOP, even if Republicans are right about how they will beat the polls.

What they actually need is for those late deciders, a sliver as they may be, to break decisively for the red team. That brings us back to the overall current atmosphere in which those folks are deciding, which is … especially bad for the party in power.

articles.title: A blue wave in the midterms could tank markets
articles.summary: Are investors indifferent as to which party is in charge or are they simply tuning out all the dire projections of losses by Republicans?
articles.body:
With the liberal press joyfully predicting that Democrats will take over the House and possibly the Senate in the November midterms, why aren’t investors pricing in a likely U-turn on some of President Trump’s pro-business agenda? Or worse — a slowdown in the AI juggernaut that continues to drive equity markets higher?

After all, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and many of his leftist colleagues want to stop the rollout of new AI models and the building of data centers altigether at least, for now. . If they take charge of Congress, won’t the “super intelligence” companies, as Trump calls them, be in trouble?

Stuart Kaiser, head of U.S. equity trading at Citi, recently told a Fox Business audience that options markets show Election Day to be the biggest event moving the stock market currently — bigger even than interest rates.

But on the day Kaiser spoke, markets were bursting through all-time record highs , even as headlines, backed up by polling, were predicting a blue wave on Election Day. Betting site Polymarket puts the odds of Republicans losing the House at 90 percent, and Democrats gaining control of the Senate at 60 percent. Just weeks ago, that site had Republicans keeping the upper chamber.

Dan Clifton, head of policy research at Baird Strategas, cautions that “Republican Senate campaigns … are in a near panic mode.” He points to similar circumstances in 2006: “a second-term Republican president with an unpopular Middle East war and high gasoline prices thought the party could maintain the Senate,” but “one month later Democrats won 30 House seats, 6 Senate seats, and 6 gubernatorial races.”

Are investors indifferent to which party is in charge or are they simply tuning out all the dire projections of losses by Republicans?

For sure, political swings can impact markets. The election of Trump to the Oval Office in 2016 and again in 2024 caused stocks to surge, for good reason. The president campaigned on pro-growth measures like lower taxes, promoting energy independence and lighter regulations, among other issues such as securing the border. In the six weeks that followed his 2016 election, the S&P 500 rose 6 percent and gained 21 percent over the ensuing year . Markets greeted Trump’s 2024 win with a 4.6 percent jump, and gained 17.5 percent over the next year.

Of course, markets do not always cheer an incoming president . Six weeks after Barack Obama was elected president in 2008, markets had sold off 9.2 percent , and the next-day response to Obama’s victories was negative in both 2008 and 2012.

In a note earlier this year, Bank of America wrote that stocks have moved higher after every postwar midterm, with the fourth quarter posting the best results of the year. Specifically, the bank notes that since World War II, the S&P index has risen in every six- and 12-month period after a midterm, on average by 13 percent and 14 percent , respectively. Maybe that’s why investors are somewhat nonchalant.

And yet this cycle could be especially bruising for businesses and for equity markets.

The Democratic Party has been infiltrated by radical far-left elements hostile to many of our leading industries. Likely wins by candidates like Democratic Socialist of America Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-N.Y.), running in New York’s deep-blue 13th congressional district, will add to the number of far-left members of the House who aspire to smash America’s capitalist economy and embrace socialist measures like Medicare for All and universal housing. Chevalier also opposes Israel and has called the U.S. a “f—ing disgrace,” once claiming in a since-deleted X post, “I forgot to get napkins so I just wiped my hand on the American flag behind me.”

These people will not be easy to manage. There are seven self-described democratic socialists running for Congress this year ; most won primaries in districts where their election is practically guaranteed. They will join Sanders, Rep. Alexandria-Ocasio Cortez (D-N.Y.) and others who make up the Progressive Caucus, a group of about 100 lawmakers — nearly half the Democrats in the House.

Like the right-wing of the Republican Party, they will punch above their weight. If Democrats achieve only a narrow majority in the House, which appears likely , the leadership will need their votes to legislate, as current Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has had to rely on his party’s fractious Freedom Caucus on numerous occasions. That means concessions will have to be made. A few hard-left House members could block spending for the military, push for new bank regulations or demand safeguards around AI that could slow that industry’s progress.

Despite investors appearing sanguine about the Republicans continuing to control the Senate, Clifton claims that “equities (have been) pricing in a Dem sweep since August 1.” Industries like banks and defense companies likely to be targeted by the left have indeed trailed the market over the past three months, but continued gains by semiconductor companies and other AI-related firms, which some analysts say comprise as much as half of the S&P 500, show investors may not be ready for a possible blue wave.

It isn’t just stocks that could be hurt by Democrats’ hostility toward AI. The industry is also fueling an investment and construction boom, boosting economic expansion and blue-collar hiring. Productivity gains and corporate profits could be crushed by adverse regulations.

It is possible that the left’s anti-AI and anti-data center protests are just political posturing. But given what’s at stake — for the country and for stocks — a blue wave could get ugly.

Liz Peek is a former partner of major bracket Wall Street firm Wertheim and Company.

articles.title: ‘Expect deaths in that plant’: Former employees describe hazardous conditions at Chinese-owned Ohio plant
articles.summary: Former Fuyao Glass America workers described unbearable heat, anti-union threats, and safety failures at the Dayton, Ohio, factory to Rep. Ro Khanna.
articles.body: A Chinese glass manufacturer’s decision not to comply with a congressional oversight inquiry prompted Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., to convene a revealing roundtable with the plant’s former workers, where they described a series of hazardous work conditions and fears for their safety. Khanna, the ranking member on the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), first reached out to Fuyao Glass America and its Chinese parent company Fuyao Glass Industry Group Co., Ltd. in July, requesting documents detailing the company’s business and labor practices. Fuyao quickly drew the attention of Americans in the Rust Belt and beyond when it became the subject of the 2019 Netflix documentary "American Factory," which chronicled its takeover of a former General Motors plant outside of Dayton, Ohio. LAWMAKERS PRESS DHS IN LETTER OVER CHINESE FORCED LABOR ALLEGATIONS, FLAG POPULAR LABUBU DOLLS The company has since been mired in scandals ranging from hundreds of thousands of dollars in fines to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) for workplace safety violations to the 2018 death of factory worker Ricky Patterson. In a subsequent October letter to Fuyao leadership, Khanna decried the company’s refusal to dialogue, condemning them for only sending one single letter in response to his numerous inquiries. Fuyao's Sept. 23 response, Khanna wrote in his Oct. 1 letter to the company, "answers virtually none of the Committee’s questions in a material way and fails to include any document submissions." CHINA’S INFLUENCE MACHINE: FEDERAL RECORDS EXPOSE BEIJING’S PUSH TO SWAY AMERICA Despite Fuyao’s silence, Khanna made the journey to Western Ohio, an area of the country decimated by a loss of manufacturing jobs in recent decades. Khanna convened a roundtable discussion on Tuesday involving former Fuyao employees and current union leaders at the Industrial Division of the Communications Workers of America (IUE-CWA) headquarters in Dayton, Ohio. DAVID MARCUS: IN DAYTON, OHIO, BOTH PARTIES FACE BITTER POLITICAL DESPONDENCY During the discussion, former Fuyao workers described unbearable heat, an inability to communicate with their Chinese supervisors and apparent labor violations involving their Chinese counterparts, among other grievances. "The heat in there is unbearable. They don't care," Tiffany Moore, who worked at Fuyao for three years, told the group. AMERICA’S BROKEN LEGAL IMMIGRATION SYSTEM IS REPLACING US WORKERS BY DESIGN "There's the language barrier. They can't communicate with you. When you try to communicate with them, they'll send someone else to you. Maybe one of them speaks English," Moore continued. Like many of the former Fuyao employees at the table, Moore now works at Duramax, a General Motors-owned engine manufacturer, where she says she is much happier. But to even apply for the position she had to employ clandestine measures to avoid retaliation from her Fuyao bosses. I'M THE ACTING SECRETARY OF LABOR AND I'M HERE TO SAY THANK YOU TO THE AMERICAN WORKER "You can't put your two weeks in because if you put your two weeks, they'll get rid of you before your two weeks come up for any reason. They'll tell you they don't have to have a reason to get rid of you just so that they can fill your position. So when I left there, I had to actually sneak out, do my orientation at DMAX. And then call them and tell them that I wasn't coming back and for them to release my 401k," Moore said. Demetria Hodges, another worker who fled Fuyao for Duramax, recounted the time a Chinese forklift driver, who she believed to be unlicensed, struck her with the machine and faced no accountability. WELDER TURNED LAWMAKER SEES A ‘NUCLEAR BOMB FOR WORK’ — AND A CHANCE TO HELP BLUE COLLAR AMERICANS "It was on camera, they have cameras in there, and they acted like they didn’t know who the forklift driver was," she told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview. "So when I tried to pursue a lawsuit and my workman’s comp, they pretended like they didn’t know who the person was." While the American workers described abysmal conditions for themselves, they said the Chinese workers were treated even worse. WHAT THE GOLF CART INDUSTRY CAN TEACH US ABOUT CHINA’S THREAT TO AMERICAN JOBS "They were treated horrible," Moore told the group. "They weren't allowed to take anything from us. They weren't really allowed to communicate with us. They weren't allowed to mix with us." Moore, Hodges and others said the Chinese workers were almost always the ones chosen for promotions because Fuyao could pay them less. They also said the company was constantly busing in new workers from elsewhere. CORPORATE AMERICA'S CHINA ADDICTION HAS BECOME A NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT "They used to rotate them out every couple months. Like they will go to New York and get a bus for or a van full of people and bring them down here. And they work for a certain amount of months, and then they rotate and send them back," Hodges said. When Hodges explained that workers were still forced to come to work the day after part of the factory caught fire, Khanna asked her if the workers were undocumented. "I believe that's why they accepted it because they were undocumented," Hodges said. Darrell Jones, another former Fuyao employee, told Khanna he felt the workers needed a union backing them, a point which quickly drew heated commentary from the group. "They wouldn't let a union come in there," Moore chimed in. "You couldn't even speak of a union being in there." "Or you could lose your job," Hodges added. Jones went on to explain that Fuyao threatened employees, telling them the company would take away their health insurance if they unionized. Hodges then added that the company offered employees a one-time pay bump of $2 an hour if they voted no on a planned unionization referendum. "They said if we ever get a union there, he was going to shut it down," Jones recalled a supervisor telling him. Jones also recalled the circumstances that led up to the tragic 2018 death of 57-year-old Fuyao factory worker Ricky Patterson. "When that guy got smashed by that glass, we had to work that day," Jones recounted. "He was a little shaky because he had just lost his mom. He was trying load up to glass. He cut one end of it. And then he was supposed to put the forklift in front of it, but he didn't put the forklift in front of it. When he cut that first side, the other side was loose," Jones said. "Crushed him," he concluded. OSHA fined Fuyao $7,000 in an informal settlement for a safety violation that led to Patterson's death. "There's a guy used to work there, he passed away, he used to tell me all the time, he said he told you guys that 'you ought to be able to expect deaths in that plant,'" Sam Sanders, the president of IUE-CWA's local Dayton chapter told the group. "He said what?" someone asked. "Expect deaths in that plant," Sanders reiterated. Khanna told the group he thought America needed new standards for foreign businesses purchasing or building factories in the U.S., a point he reiterated during an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital. "We can welcome foreign investment in the United States of America, we should if they want to open factories, but they have to play by our rules. They have to do things, not like they do in foreign countries, but like they do in America," Khanna told Fox News Digital. "That means having safety standards. That means safety standards that are enforced. That means labor neutrality, so you can't have anti-union campaigns. That means complying with anti-discrimination laws based on gender and race. That means having communication where workers have a voice, that you can treat workers is dispensable," he continued. The Silicon Valley congressman went on to explain that he hoped to be able to craft legislation that would reform the current process that allows foreign companies to purchase U.S. factories without much oversight. He also argued that American manufacturing needs a boost from the U.S. government. "We need an industrial development bank in the United States that invests in places like Dayton, Ohio, to build new factories, to support manufacturers who are making things which we're currently importing. Why are we just relying on foreign investment?" he asked. After not being granted an oversight look into the Fuyao factory itself, Khanna still wanted to get a look at the plant from outside, stopping to pose for a picture just a few feet off of company property. "We need to understand how they're setting standards. We need to understand how they are complying with American labor law. We need to understand what the impact of foreign investment is so that we can craft legislation to address the issue," Khanna told Fox News Digital. "I'm disappointed they aren't complying because it's not in any way a gotcha issue. Legislators need this information to be able to address the issue," he said. "Everyone should want good jobs where American national security is protected, and American standards are protected," Khanna concluded.
